brief: Per Morgan Stanley, the top 20% of US households hold $49.8tn in equity wealth against $8.3tn in labor income, while the bottom 40% holds $1.8tn in labor income versus $1.7tn in equity wealth. The top 10% owns 87% of corporate equities and mutual funds while representing 10% of households, and essentials fall from 59% of spending for the bottom 20% to 38% for the top 20%. For the cohort that spends most, consumption tracks the equity market more than the paycheck. At the same time, equity gains concentrate in AI: Goldman's US Discretionary basket has fallen to 86.6 versus AI from above 105 earlier this year, low-income discretionary sits at 93.7, and Goldman's Consumer Inertia Index has fallen from 100.56 in January to 85.39. JPM finds retail turnover in the AI/Datacenter/Electrification basket up 56.54% YTD. Morgan Stanley finds high-AI-exposure occupations carry median salaries of $81,680 unweighted and $96,690 employment-weighted, versus $48,680 and $46,390 for low-exposure occupations, meaning the jobs most exposed to AI are disproportionately the high-paying jobs held by the wealth-effect cohort. The note frames this as a loop and asks what happens to consumption if AI erodes those same jobs.
